## 2. `openspec/changes/control-plane-in-dash/`

Files: `proposal.md`, `design.md`, `tasks.md`, `specs/platform-self-management/spec.md`, `.openspec.yaml` (`schema: spec-driven`, created 2026-08-02).

### (a) Design decisions

| # | One-line summary | Depends on "repo lives in dash env"? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Dividing line: inside dash = what you author; on the host = what keeps things alive; test = apps still serve + platform still repairable with dash down. | Framing depends; the test is independent. |
| 2 | Why each unmoved thing stays out: machine lifecycle (host-only `orb`), tunnel (dash outage would kill all URLs), model (needs Metal), secrets (no added capability, bigger blast radius). | Independent. |
| 3 | dash gets **no** reach into other envs at all — reversal of the earlier `tag:control` tailnet grant; fleet ops go through the daemon's `in_machine()`; root ssh everywhere would falsify the privilege requirement. | Independent. |
| 4 | Repo lives in **both** places; GitHub is the sync point; host clone is break-glass only; three legibility devices: (a) `ROLE` file per checkout, (b) repo organized by execution site `bin/`/`golden/`/`fleet/`/`openspec/`, (c) `/app` = the dashboard app vs `/app/platform` = the platform. | **Entirely dependent.** |
| 5 | dash can **author** host-side code but not **deploy** it; no self-update endpoint, because it would let dash rewrite what the daemon permits. | Privilege half independent; "authored in dash" half dependent. |
| 6 | Fleet operations are offered per environment, never applied wholesale; report of changed/skipped/failed; no apply-to-all mode. | Independent. |
| 7 | Fleet operations are **named** host-implemented operations invoked from dash (bounded catalogue, not generic exec); notes that this + Decision 8 are deltas to `platform-control-api`, owned by the in-flight `platform-dashboard` change → groups 4/5 gated. | Independent (but internally inconsistent with tasks.md 5.1, see note below). |
| 8 | Golden stays **off** the tailnet (clone would inherit identity); baseline rebuild is host-mediated; `join_tailnet()` gains `--force-reauth`; `bounce` re-auth escalation remains open as `platform-dashboard` task 6.2. | Independent (only "recipe in `/app/platform`" phrasing is dependent). |
| 9 | Self-modification safety: dashboard stays a single static file, `serve.py` separate from the page, dash never the only repair path. | Mostly independent. |

Note on an internal inconsistency: Decision 7 and the proposal's "What Changes" say fleet ops run **through the daemon** with no dash reach, while `tasks.md` 5.1 says a fleet primitive is "a script in `/app/platform` run **from dash over ssh**, no new host surface (design Decision 6)" — and `fleet/README.md` says the host executes on the control app's behalf. The proposal's Impact section also says "Fleet operations need no new host surface; they run from the control app over ssh," contradicting its own bullet two paragraphs above.

### (b) Capability: `platform-self-management` (ADDED — 7 requirements)

| Requirement | One-line summary | Depends on repo-in-dash? |
|---|---|---|
| The platform is editable from within itself | Specs, baseline recipe, fleet ops, and the control app's source are readable/editable inside the control app's env and take effect with no host session; host-executed code is the sole exception. | **Yes — wholly.** (3 scenarios: phone edit of the baseline; specs travel with the control app; host code authored inside/applied outside.) |
| The control app cannot expand its own privileges | The privileged operation set is determined outside the control app; nothing lets it make the host run code of its choosing. (Scenarios: boundary not editable from inside; no self-update path offered.) | No. |
| The control plane is not required for the platform to run | Apps keep serving with the control app stopped, and a non-control-app repair route exists and is exercised. (Scenarios: apps outlive control plane; broken control plane still repairable.) | No (the *mirror* is an implementation of it, but the requirement stands alone). |
| Self-management does not weaken existing guarantees | Baseline changes made from inside behave like any other: only new envs affected, none re-applied (cites `openspec/specs/app-environments/spec.md`). | No. |
| Fleet operations are offered, never imposed | Per-env explicit decision required; per-env changed/skipped/failed report; no apply-to-everything mode. (3 scenarios.) | No. |
| The control app acts on environments only through a bounded catalogue | No direct access into other envs; only named host-offered operations, no caller-supplied code; app-to-app also closed. (4 scenarios.) | No. |
| The control app holds no platform secrets | Only the control-interface bearer token lives there; provider credentials stay outside. | No. |

Modified capabilities are **declared but not written**: the proposal states `platform-control-api` (+ baseline rebuild) and `dashboard-ui` (+ spec-review panel) are owned by the in-flight `platform-dashboard` change, so no delta files exist here; groups 4 and 8 are gated on `platform-dashboard` archiving.

Task state: groups 1, 2, 3, 7.1/7.2 and 6.1 are checked `[x]`; groups 4, 5, 6.2, 7.3, 8 are open.

---

## 3. `openspec/changes/platform-dashboard/`

### `platform-control-api` (ADDED — 7 requirements) — all **SERVER contract**

| Requirement | Summary |
|---|---|
| Only authorized callers are served | Every request needs the bearer token; missing/wrong → 401 and no state change. |
| App inventory reflects live state | Authorized inventory returns name, URL, visibility, env run-state, port, tailnet reachability matching reality (incl. running-but-unreachable). |
| Lifecycle operations preserve existing guarantees | API create/remove behave identically to `openspec/specs/app-lifecycle/spec.md` (name validation, collision refusal, gate-before-route, placeholder, repo preserved). |
| Policy operations apply access-gating semantics | Sets exactly one of public/allowlist(emails)/owner, per `openspec/specs/access-gating/spec.md`, within 5 min, with no app-process change. |
| Env control actions | start / stop / bounce supported; inventory reflects the resulting run-state and restored reachability. |
| Host secrets never leave the host | No response (success or error) contains the CF token, tailnet keys, or the control token. |
| Model service surface | Reports model health; wake returns only when healthy or on timeout error. |

### `dashboard-ui` (ADDED — 5 requirements) — all **CLIENT UI**

| Requirement | Summary |
|---|---|
| All apps at a glance | Gated phone-reachable page listing every app with URL, visibility, run-state; auto-refresh ≤15 s picks up out-of-band changes. |
| Visibility is a tap, not a terminal | Public / allowlist+emails / owner-only changeable purely in-page, reflected after next refresh. |
| Create and remove from the page | New-app name field creates; card removal works and messaging states the repository is preserved. |
| Tap-to-shell | Each card offers a shell link opening the device SSH client at `root@<env tailnet name>`. |
| Platform health strip | Model health + wake action, and per-env reachability + bounce for unreachable envs, all without a terminal. |

Design decisions here (6): privilege split UI-container + `apphostd` on 127.0.0.1:8092; static bearer token at `~/.config/apphost/control-token` injected only into dash; `appctl` → `appctl_lib.py` + thin CLI shared by daemon; the JSON API shape/response contract; single static vanilla-JS card page polling every 10 s; dash is a normal `newapp` app whose only specialness is `CONTROL_TOKEN`. Two runtime notes at the top correct the container-era text: envs are OrbStack machines, and the daemon is reached at `host.orb.internal`, not `host.docker.internal`.

---

## 4. Physical artifacts group-3 created (reversal surface)

- Relevant commits: `8755a72` (ROLE, fleet/, README layout, envs/ removal, force-reauth), `6e9df21` (README break-glass step 6 + tasks.md check-offs), `e86963a` (fish in `bin/build-golden`, group 6).

**Inside the dash machine** (`orb -m dash -u root ls -la /app /app/platform`):

```
/app:      .git/  README.md  index.html  platform/  run  serve.py
/app/platform:  .DS_Store  .claude/  .git/  .gitignore  .obsidian/
                README.md  ROLE  bin/  fleet/  golden/  openspec/
```

- `/app/platform` is a **full second clone** of the repo (`origin https://github.com/toejough/phone-llm.git`), owned `joe:staff`, seeded 2026-08-02 17:22.
- `/app/platform/ROLE` says `working-copy` / "This is the authoritative checkout… The host keeps a pull-only mirror at ~/repos/personal/phone-llm".
- `/app/platform/fleet/` also contains only `README.md`.
- **Drift exists in both directions right now:** dash is at `3251be5 chore: this checkout is the working copy`, `## main...origin/main [ahead 1]` (unpushed — no `gh auth` in dash per task 3.3), and it does **not** have the host's later `6e9df21` and `e86963a`. ## 5. What dash's own `/app` repo tracks

```
$ orb -m dash -u root bash -c 'cd /app && git ls-files && git status --porcelain | head -20'
index.html
```

## Step 0: Adversarial Review Stance

**Ask:** Does this proposal remain consistent with existing OpenSpec documentation, retain all original requirement text before modifications, avoid contradictions with staying capabilities, and comprehensively address all places where the old architecture is currently documented?

**Situation:** The proposal reverses a two-checkout arrangement by moving the platform repo back to host-only. The current README, ROLE file, break-glass procedure, and task documentation across multiple changes document the two-checkout architecture extensively. The proposal modifies app-environments and app-lifecycle capabilities while introducing a new platform-client-boundary capability. Two in-flight changes (platform-dashboard and control-plane-in-dash) are being split/narrowed and archived.

**Plan for adversarial review:**
1. Verify the app-environments modification reproduces entire original requirement verbatim before edits
2. Search for contradictions with requirements in app-lifecycle, access-gating, public-ingress  
3. Grep existing docs for every architectural claim the change reverses

5. Verify capability boundaries are clear between platform-client-boundary and platform-control-api

## Finding 1: STALE CLAIM IN README.md (HIGH SEVERITY)

**Location:** `/Users/joe/repos/personal/phone-llm/README.md:122`

```
see the drill notes in the archived `control-plane-in-dash` change.
```

Format is correct (### for Requirements, #### for Scenarios). Now let me verify SHALL/MUST language and identify the critical testability issue:

The analysis is complete. Here are my findings, ranked by severity:

---

## FINDINGS (Ranked by Severity)

### CRITICAL: Scenario combines four independent claims — untestable as written

**File:** `specs/app-environments/spec.md`, lines 22–25

**Scenario:** "What the platform depends on still works"

```
#### Scenario: What the platform depends on still works
- **WHEN** isolation is in force
- **THEN** the environment still reaches the platform's local model service 
  and the public internet, the owner still reaches it by shell over the tailnet, 
  and its app is still served at its public URL — isolation removes host and 
  neighbour access without removing the platform
```

**Problem:** One THEN asserts four unrelated things:
1. Environment reaches model service
2. Environment reaches internet  
3. Owner reaches via shell over tailnet
4. App served at public URL

If any one fails, the scenario fails without telling you which. A test failure gives no signal. Worse, item 3 (owner reaching by shell) is about host behavior, not environment isolation—it doesn't belong here.

**Rewrite proposal:**

```
#### Scenario: Model service and internet survive isolation
- **WHEN** an environment is isolated
- **THEN** it still reaches the platform's local model service and the public internet

#### Scenario: Public ingress survives isolation
- **WHEN** an app's environment is isolated
- **THEN** its public URL still serves incoming requests

#### Scenario: Host shell access survives isolation
- **WHEN** isolation is in force
- **THEN** the owner can still ssh to the host and reach the app by shell over the tailnet
```

Separating them makes each a concrete command with an expected result.

---

### MAJOR: Task group 4 numbering is incoherent

**File:** `tasks.md`, lines 47–74

Group 4 starts at **4.0**, not **4.1**. All other groups start at .1 (1.1, 2.1, 3.1, 5.1). The break is visible:

```
## 4. Close the control interface...

- [ ] 4.0 Decide the transport by measuring...    ← Should be 4.1
- [ ] 4.1 The daemon's listener moves...          ← Should be 4.2
- [ ] 4.2 The dashboard's control URL...          ← Should be 4.3
- [ ] 4.3 Verify the cases...                     ← Should be 4.4
- [ ] 4.4 (Joe, or a second device)...            ← Should be 4.5
```

This is either a late insertion that wasn't tidied, or 4.0 was meant to signal a decision task rather than implementation—but then why is 4.1 implementation? Renumber to 4.1–4.5 for consistency.

---

### MAJOR: Design Decision 2 is verbose and defensive

**File:** `design.md`, lines 74–101

The justification for tailnet over bridge spans ~25 lines and repeats the macOS Local Network privacy incident multiple times. The structure is defensive—arguing around the bridge option rather than asserting the tailnet choice:

```
**Where it moves to is not the bridge interface, on this platform's own evidence.** 
The `dash-as-client` planning settled on the bridge; recall surfaced a measured record 
that argues against it. This platform has already collided with macOS Local Network privacy: 
`cloudflared` under launchd could not reach OrbStack machine addresses at all — not by name, 
not by raw IP — while a launchd-spawned `curl` reached the same address and returned 200...
```

**Concise rewrite:**

```
**Tailnet, not bridge.** Prior platform work hit macOS Local Network privacy: `cloudflared` 
under launchd could not reach OrbStack addresses (per-binary TCC), but switching to the 
tailnet fixed it. `apphostd` is also launchd-managed; the bridge plan puts it back in 
that neighbourhood. The tailnet provides stable MagicDNS names instead of hardcoded IPs 
and reuses the transport ingress and ssh already trust. Caveat: tailnet paths can wedge 
after machine recreation, but the dashboard's ingress already rides the tailnet—not a new 
failure mode. Task 4.0 measures both before committing.
```

This cuts the section in half and removes defensive repetition while preserving the evidence.

---

### MODERATE: Tasks 1.3, 2.2, and 4.3 use activity language instead of outcome language

**File:** `tasks.md`

The user's standards call for verifiable outcomes. Three tasks state activities:

1. **Line 13–15, Task 1.3:** `"The claim is tested from inside, not from the config"`
   - Activity language ("tested")
   - **Rewrite:** `"From each environment, attempting to read ~/.ssh/id_rsa, ~/.config/gh/hosts.yml, and ~/.config/apphost/control-token all fail, and resolving another app's name fails"`

2. **Line 28–29, Task 2.2:** `"Prove it on a throwaway app created through the ordinary path..."`
   - Activity language ("prove")
   - **Rewrite:** `"A new app created through the ordinary path has no /mnt/mac, cannot reach neighbours, and still serves"`

3. **Line 64–67, Task 4.3:** Combines four test cases without clear separation
   - Tests dashboard auth, non-granted env rejection, host-like routing, and daemon failure separately—but phrased as one task
   - **Rewrite:** Either split into separate tasks (4.3a–d) or reframe as: `"The control interface accepts the dashboard's credential, refuses other environments even with valid credentials, is not reachable via host-spoofing routes, and appctl works when the daemon is stopped"`

---

### MODERATE: Severity framing could be sharper

**File:** `proposal.md`, lines 26–29 and the closing of design.md

The proposal is appropriately plain about the exposure but could be more direct about the risk level. Currently:
- "has had the keys to everything for as long as the platform has existed" (dramatic, justified)
- "There is no evidence of compromise" (appropriate)

But the framing mixes appropriate severity with some hedging. Compare to dash-as-client's framing (which directly states "is not actually privileged" and acknowledges the problem plainly). Here, the severity is buried in the middle rather than leading the piece. The proposal's "Why" section is strong, but "no evidence of compromise" could be more decisive: *"The window was open; acting as though it was not is the risk, not checking if it was exploited."*

---

### MINOR: Proposal "What Changes" repeats design Decisions

**File:** `proposal.md`, lines 31–45 vs. `design.md`, lines 34–105

The proposal's four-point "What Changes" is largely restated in design's four Decisions. This is normal (proposal summarizes, design elaborates), but some sentences appear in both:

- Proposal line 33: *"OrbStack has a per-machine `isolated` setting; turning it on removes `/mnt/mac` entirely."*
- Design line 37: *"`orb config set machine.<name>.isolated true`, then restart."*

These are slightly different (goal vs. mechanism), so not truly redundant, but the proposal could tighten by removing the mechanism details—those belong in the design. Keep the proposal to *what* and *why*; leave *how* to the design.

---

### MINOR: "Explicitly not in scope" at proposal end could be clearer

**File:** `proposal.md`, lines 67–71

The final section lists what's deliberately out of scope but uses permissive language ("deliberately out", "only makes sense once"). Could be more direct:

```
Scoped host-directory sharing is not included. OrbStack's `mounts` setting is the 
mechanism; it only makes sense once the default is closed. Task 6.1 reopens this after 
isolation lands.
```

- **OpenSpec format compliance:** All requirements use 3 hashes (###), all scenarios use 4 hashes (####). ✓
- **SHALL/MUST language:** Consistent throughout both spec files. No "should" or "may" in requirements. ✓
- **File-to-file consistency:** Proposal, design, tasks, and specs align on scope, decisions, and what's exposed. No contradictions. ✓
- **Rotation decision:** Correctly split (rotate control token; name the others and let Joe decide). Consistent across all files. ✓
- **Scenario testability** (except the one noted above): Conflicting dependencies, no host filesystem, no reach between apps, control interface boundary—each is a concrete, checkable command. ✓

completion_report:
## Verification: the revised host-side enforcement mechanism (unix socket + bridge TCP)

I re-read the live `design.md`/`tasks.md` (they've already been updated to the text you described — Decision 2, tasks 2.1–2.2) and ran the following against the actual system, read-only, no restarts or rebinds.

### 1. Is the bridge address stable *and* addressable by name? — **No name exists; this is the design's real weak point**

```
orb -m hello -u root getent ahostsv4 host.orb.internal   -> 0.250.250.254
orb -m hello -u root getent hosts host.orb.internal      -> fd07:b51a:cc66:f0::fe
orb -m hello -u root getent hosts gateway.orb.internal    -> fd07:b51a:cc66:f0::1
orb -m hello -u root getent hosts host.docker.internal    -> 0.250.250.254
orb -m hello -u root getent hosts bridge.orb.internal / orb.internal / orbstack.internal -> (nothing)
```
`host.orb.internal`, `host.docker.internal`, and `gateway.orb.internal` all live in a **separate magic-gateway subnet** (`0.250.250.0/24`-ish / `fd07:b51a:cc66:f0::/64`, note prefix segment `f0`) — this is a different address family from the bridge's real subnet (`192.168.139.0/23` / `fd07:b51a:cc66:0::/64`, segment `0`). This is *why* traffic through `host.orb.internal` always shows up as `127.0.0.1` to a loopback-bound service: it's relayed through this dedicated gateway subnet, not routed directly to the bridge. **No name resolves to the bridge address from inside a machine.** I checked the obvious candidates and none exist.

This confirms your suspicion exactly: dash's `CONTROL_URL` will have to target the literal bridge IP (`192.168.139.3`), not a name. That is a genuine, new fragility the design doesn't currently name as a task. I found no DNS-based escape from it. Crystallized as vault note `708.2026-08-02.orbstack-magic-hostnames-not-bridge-address.md`.

On stability of that literal IP: I found real historical evidence, not just inference. `~/.orbstack/log/vmgr.1.log`'s last line is a kernel `reboot: Power down` / `VM stopped` at `08-01 12:18:51`; `vmgr.log` (the next generation) begins at `08-01 12:18:56` — a genuine full OrbStack VM-manager restart. A machine that came up *after* that restart (`apphost-golden`, logged at `08-01 16:29:09`) still landed on `192.168.139.113` — same subnet as before. So the `192.168.139.0/23` network (and by extension the host's own `.3` gateway address) survived a real engine restart in this system's own history, without me needing to trigger anything. That's reassuring for the "does it move" half of the question; it does not remove the "there's no name for it" half.

**Recommendation:** add a task that pins the literal bridge IP into dash's creation-time config (task 3.2 territory) and states explicitly what happens if OrbStack ever changes its default subnet (fresh install, factory reset, or an OrbStack update) — today that would silently strand dash's `CONTROL_URL` with no re-discovery path.

### 2. Does bridge100 exist reliably across restarts? — **Yes, by the same evidence as above**

```
ifconfig bridge100 -> member: vmenet0 only
```
Beyond the vmgr-restart evidence in #1, `~/.orbstack/vmconfig.json` is `{}` and `vmstate.json` carries no network state — meaning OrbStack doesn't appear to persist the subnet choice as visible config; it's presumably a fixed default baked into the app. I can't prove it's *permanently* fixed without a fresh install, but the interface (`bridge100`) and its subnet demonstrably survived the one real VM-manager restart recorded in this system's logs. A prior vault note (`696`, from an earlier session) independently recorded "OrbStack machine IPs measured stable across stop/start and across an orb restart" — consistent with what I found here.

### 3. Does the bridge widen exposure to the LAN? — **Not currently, but the design should say so explicitly, and I could not fully rule it out**

```
ifconfig -a | grep -E "^bridge|member"
  bridge0:   member: en1, en2, en3       <- a DIFFERENT bridge (physical/Thunderbolt-style)
  bridge100: member: vmenet0             <- OrbStack's bridge, ONLY a virtual member
```
`bridge100` has no physical/LAN-facing interface as a member — it's topologically isolated from `en0` (Wi-Fi/Ethernet, `10.0.0.73`). That's the good news. The caveat: `sysctl net.inet.ip.forwarding` returned `1` (forwarding enabled system-wide). I couldn't inspect `pfctl` state (`Permission denied` without sudo) to rule out a NAT/forwarding rule that could expose the subnet inbound from the LAN — I found no evidence one exists, and forwarding=1 is far more plausibly explained by OrbStack's own *outbound* NAT (VM→internet) than any inbound path, but I can't certify its absence without root. **This should be verified with an actual second device on the LAN attempting `curl http://192.168.139.3:8092` before this ships** — I don't have such a device available in this session. If it's LAN-reachable, your point stands: the peer check becomes the only thing between the control plane and the whole home network, and that risk statement belongs in the design regardless of the test's outcome.

### 4. Does the unix-socket move break anything? — **Yes, or at least: it's not what it's described as, and that matters**

Enumerated every actual caller of port 8092:
```
grep -n "8092" across bin/, golden/, dash's serve.py, README.md, openspec/**
```
- `bin/apphostd` — defines the port (the daemon itself).
- `bin/appctl` — **zero references.** I read the whole file: it does `import appctl_lib as lib` and calls `lib.create_app()`, `lib.inventory()`, `lib.remove_app()` **in-process**. No `urllib`, no `socket`, no HTTP, no token, no daemon dependency at all, today.
- `bin/appctl_lib.py`, `bin/votek-ensured`, `golden/pi/*` — their `127.0.0.1`/`host.orb.internal` matches are all for the *model* service (ports 8090/8091), unrelated to apphostd.
- The **only live network client of :8092 today is `/app/serve.py` inside the `dash` machine** — an *untracked* file (per finding #3 from round one), using `CONTROL_URL`/`CONTROL_TOKEN` from the hand-placed systemd drop-in.

This means design.md's framing — "the host's CLI reaches the daemon over a unix domain socket... this also keeps the break-glass path working" — describes swapping a transport that **does not currently exist**. `appctl` isn't moving from TCP-loopback to a unix socket; it would be gaining a daemon dependency it has never had. That's a materially different (and riskier) change than the prose suggests, because it collides with a load-bearing property this same repo already documents: the README's break-glass section states the host CLI "does not need dash, the daemon's HTTP surface, or a browser," and `control-plane-in-dash`'s Decision 1 test is "if the control app is down, can the platform still be repaired?" If `appctl`'s existing create/list/remove path gets rerouted through `apphostd` via the socket, then a stuck or crashed `apphostd` — today totally irrelevant to `appctl` — becomes a new single point of failure for the repair tool itself.

To be fair to the plan: task 2.1 already says "verify the break-glass path still works over the new socket before removing the old listener" — so the authors are aware this needs checking. My finding is that the verification needs to be sharper than it currently reads: it should explicitly test `appctl create/list/remove` **with `apphostd` stopped/killed**, not just "the socket path works," because the thing being protected is "the CLI works when the daemon doesn't," not merely "the CLI can reach the daemon a different way." As written, the task could pass a test that never actually removes the daemon from the loop.

Socket/LaunchAgent mechanics check out fine on their own: `dev.toejough.apphostd.plist` has no `UserName` key, confirming it's a LaunchAgent running as `joe` in the normal login session (same user `appctl` runs as), so filesystem-permission trust is sound and there's an obvious, already-used location pattern for the socket file (`~/.config/apphost/`, currently holding `control-token` at `0600`). No permission obstacle there.

### 5. Simpler mechanism? — **I didn't find one; the rejections hold up**

I checked each rejection against what I verified live, not just the prose:
- **Per-environment token** — correctly rejected: it authenticates the credential, not reachability; every machine can still connect and probe. Consistent with what's already proven (all three machines get past the TCP handshake to :8092 today).
- **`pf` rule on 8092** — correctly rejected as primary: it's invisible to the daemon (can't self-report the grant holder) and is a second piece of host state to keep in sync with app lifecycle — consistent with the DHCP/MAC instability precedent already documented in this repo (`orb export`/`import` identity collisions).
- **mTLS / per-environment token** — same authentication-vs-reachability distinction, correctly rejected.
- **Tailnet-based reachability** — correctly rejected: I confirmed via `ip -brief addr` that `hello`, `todo`, and `dash` **all already have `tailscale0` interfaces**, so routing over the tailnet would narrow nothing.
- **Second daemon inside dash** — an architectural judgment consistent with the change's whole premise; not a technical claim to refute.

None of the five rejections are wrong. I did not find a genuinely simpler alternative that gives a real reachability boundary with one listener — a same-host TCP connection to the daemon's own bridge IP would reintroduce exactly the "which address really means host" ambiguity the redesign exists to close, so collapsing back to one listener trades away the property being bought. The two-listener split looks close to the minimal correct answer given OrbStack's re-origination behavior.

---

**Bottom line:** the bridge-TCP half of the mechanism is sound and matches verified reality (peer addresses do survive there, the interface is topologically off the LAN, the subnet has survived a real restart in this system's history). The two things that need to change before this ships: **(a)** there is no name for the bridge address — the design needs to say plainly that dash's `CONTROL_URL` becomes a hardcoded IP with a stated recovery story if it ever moves, and **(b)** the unix-socket half is being described as a transport swap for an existing coupling that doesn't exist — `appctl` has zero dependency on `apphostd` today — so task 2.1's break-glass verification needs to specifically prove the daemon can be down/crashed and `appctl`'s core operations still work, not just that the socket path functions.

# Decisions the owner must make

Ordered. The first three gate most of what follows.

## 1. Who is the consumer — your ssh session, or the app's unattended agent?

Task 6.1 says "an app environment reading the engram vault" and every subsequent analysis read that as *the coding agent, with standing ambient access*. That reading is what generates the multi-tenant grant, the per-app allowlist, the `golden/FILES` optionality problem, the endpoint-delivery vehicle, and the `CLOSED_PORTS` category. But the reason you want recall in an env is arguably that **you** work there — `README.md:87-96` documents phone-ssh as the primary way in. Peer identity cannot distinguish the two: `bin/apphostd:131` checks `self.client_address[0] in granted_addrs()`, so you typing `/recall` in `hello` and a prompt-injected agent in `hello` present the identical tailnet peer. Under engram#720 both write notes stamped `hello` — and your own vault-authored content is the higher-confidence tier in your memory model.

**Recommendation:** answer this before working any other decision. If the dominant want is owner-session access, a session-scoped shape becomes available that nobody has proposed — no standing host listener, no grant file, no multi-tenancy, no `CLOSED_PORTS` entry, failing closed by construction when nobody is connected — and roughly eight decisions below collapse. Whether that shape is even buildable is OQ4. **Trading away:** session scope means an unattended agent in an env never has memory, which is a real loss for anything long-running.

## 2. Ship engram before, or behind, the cross-app reach fix?

This is the one that surprised the review. Per-app grants are **not enforceable today**, and it is worse than a leak. From `hello`, `http://192.168.139.142:8080/api/apps` returns 200 with the full platform inventory, no credential — and dash's proxy is method-agnostic: `/app/serve.py:32` `_proxy(method)` attaches `Authorization: Bearer {CONTROL_TOKEN}` at :38 and is wired to `do_GET`, `do_POST` (:64) and `do_DELETE` (:70). Any environment can create apps, delete apps, bounce another app's machine, and rewrite another app's Access policy, unauthenticated, through dash. Cross-app reach is live on four independent planes: bridge IP (`hello`→`todo` 192.168.139.140:8080 → 200), MagicDNS (`todo.tail2fbf9.ts.net:8080` → 200), the host's `*:8080` wildcard forward, and the host's LAN address (`10.0.0.73:8080` → 200, serving todo's owner-only page unauthenticated to the whole house). `fleet/check-isolation:76` reports `ok cannot resolve neighbours` because it tests `getent hosts` — name resolution, not reach. `orb config show` explains it: every machine has `isolate_network: false`. `README.md:164` asserts the opposite in prose.

Consequence for engram specifically: if it is granted to app A and closed to app B, B asks A — and because #720 stamps provenance from the authenticated caller, a proxied `learn` from B lands stamped as A. Confidently wrong provenance is worse than none, because it will be believed.

**Recommendation:** file the reach defect against phone-llm and the unauthenticated method-agnostic proxy against dash **now**, independent of engram — it is a live control-plane compromise plus a Cloudflare-Access bypass, and it should not queue behind a memory feature. Until it lands, grant engram **fleet-wide or not at all**. Do not ship a per-app grant the platform cannot back; a second control that reads as a boundary and is not one is the specific failure `fleet/check-isolation:7-10` was written against. **Trading away:** no per-app engram policy in v1, which means decision 3 collapses to "all envs or none" for the first release.

## 3. Default posture for a newly created app, and where the grant record lives

Two precedents pull opposite ways. Ports 1234 and 8091 are offered to every env anonymously, justified per-port at `fleet/check-isolation:13-31` because those services cannot tell callers apart and are built not to need to. The control interface went the other way: one recorded name in `~/.config/apphost/grant` (currently `dash`). Engram is the first host service where caller identity changes what should be returned, so the 1234/8091 precedent does not transfer.

There is nowhere to write the record. `~/.config/apphost/` holds three flat files; `inventory()` (`bin/appctl_lib.py:231-259`) derives every per-app fact at request time and stores nothing; and OrbStack's per-machine config is a fixed ten-key schema that will not take a new key. Worse, **`golden/FILES` cannot express an optional file at all**: `fleet/_baseline.py:48-59` is a flat list with no per-machine notion, `fleet/check-baseline:71-76` loops every file × every target and increments `problems` on anything not `current`, and `fleet/offer:53-59` refuses any path not listed. A file that is deliberately not universal reports permanent `DRIFT missing` — training you to ignore a check whose entire value is that non-zero means something.

**Recommendation:** **default closed**, and split delivery from access. The client binary and its wrapper go to *every* env via `golden/FILES` (keeping that list unconditional, which is its whole virtue); the **server's peer check** decides who gets answers. Default-closed costs nothing at creation — `create_app()` simply writes nothing — and mirrors `_gate_owner_only()` running before `add_route()` (`bin/appctl_lib.py:552-553`, `:571-572`): closed first, opened by a separate deliberate act. Build the record as a map `environment → {service: scope}` from the start, not a second bare-name file; the single-name grant is already at its expressive ceiling and copying it means a second migration. That same file is the decision table `check-isolation` needs (decision 11) — one artifact, two consumers. **Trading away:** an ungranted env holds a working binary that always 403s, so the wrapper must produce a legible error rather than silence; and you own a new file format plus a migration of the existing `grant`.

Note the standing constraint bites here: "offered to all" is the option that requires asking you, and it is also the option the delivery mechanism would pick by default if nobody decides.

## 4. Scope inside the grant: read-only, or read plus write?

`activate` is on #720's exposed list and it mutates retrieval state, so even a nominally read-shaped verb changes what your next `/recall` surfaces. A bare app name has no verb dimension. Write is not a smaller read: a note written from an env is durable (it outlives both machines), host-mediated (it works when the app is stopped), and read by **you** — a note written by whatever model is in `hello` lands in your next `/recall`, and confidence decay ages it rather than removing it.

**Recommendation:** start read-only, but express the record per-verb from day one even when every entry is read-only — retrofitting a dimension onto a grant file is a migration this platform has already done once. Enforcement of per-caller verb scope is engram's job; the record and its verification are yours, and you have to state the requirement or engram's API has nothing to satisfy. If writes are wanted later, the shape is quarantine: stamped with app identity, excluded from your default recall until you promote them on the host. **Trading away:** `/learn` does not follow an agent into the VM, which is half the stated goal.

## 5. Who is excluded regardless of the allowlist

Two exclusions, both structural.

**dash.** It holds the control grant, and `write_control_config()` writes `CONTROL_TOKEN` into a root-readable systemd drop-in inside that machine (`bin/appctl_lib.py:374-379`). `POST /apps/<name>/policy` → `set_policy` accepts `mode=public` for any app (`:264-277`). Give dash a vault grant and one environment holds both "read the owner's vault" and "make any app anonymously reachable from the internet" — the exfiltration chain collapsed into a single agent, no injection needed. `platform-self-management` spec.md:6-7 and :54-55 bound dash's power in terms of control-API operations and credentials; a peer-identity grant is neither, so it slips between both requirements while being exactly what they exist to prevent.

**Public apps.** `hello.toejough.dev` returns 200 unauthenticated. The full injection chain is built out of documented mechanisms and I confirmed it end to end: `GET https://hello.toejough.dev/index.html/<marker>` returned 404 and the marker appeared verbatim in `hello`'s journal three seconds later, because `golden/server/src/main.go:91-93` logs the request path on any non-`fs.ErrNotExist` error and ENOTDIR qualifies. Publishing is one command the agent already knows (`ln -s ../repo public/everything`, README.md:206-208), and there is no egress control at all.

**Recommendation:** exclude the control-grant holder in the code that writes the allowlist, not in the README — same reasoning as `write_control_config` refusing a non-granted env at `:368-369` — and add the sentence to `platform-self-management`, because the spec needs it as much as the code does. Couple the grant to Access visibility, but make the **daemon's per-request re-read** the load-bearing half, not a `set_policy()` gate: deleting an Access application in the Cloudflare console makes an app public with no code here running. Separately and cheaply, stop logging `r.URL.Path` verbatim. **Trading away:** dash's agent is the one most likely to benefit from vault access and won't have it; if that becomes painful, the answer is splitting the control grant so policy-loosening needs a host-side action dash cannot perform — a real change to a settled design, not an exception.

## 6. Read scope: whole vault, or a curated subset?

I swept the vault from first principles rather than accepting the four patterns the discussion had named — 16 credential shapes (`tskey-`, `sk-ant`, `ghp_`, `AKIA`, OpenSSH/RSA private key blocks, `ssh-rsa`/`ssh-ed25519`, `xoxb-`, `AIza`, `ya29.`, password/passwd, api_key, control-token) across the ~700 `.md` notes: **all zero**. The only hits are references, not values. What the vault does hold is a topology and incident map — 7 notes mention `host.orb.internal`, 3 mention `8092`, and titles alone are informative. So the harm from whole-vault read is reconnaissance and your private working context, not credential theft.

**Recommendation:** whole-vault read; spend the effort on the caller allowlist and the visibility coupling instead. A curated filter has to be maintained forever as 700 notes become 1000, with no signal when it falls behind — and the value of recall is precisely that you don't know in advance which note matters. Two conditions make this defensible: the credential-free property must become a **standing check** scoped to `*.md` (recursive greps hit the `.vec.json` sidecars and inflate every count — `8092` reads as 157 files instead of 3), and the cross-repo ownership has to be deliberate: the vault is engram's, so either engram owns the scanner and phone-llm requires it before granting, or phone-llm owns it as a recorded exception. **Trading away:** a granted env sees your complete working context. Note this decision was originally taken against a threat model of a 9B local model; see S8 — that premise is false, and the answer survives anyway, but the stakes are higher than they looked.

## 7. Server residency — resident-warm, wake-on-demand, or per-request

This gates supervision and concurrency, and nobody costed it. The host has 16 GiB and is at saturation right now: `PhysMem: 15G used (2740M wired, 4343M compressor), 114M unused` (verified). The model service pins ~9.5GB permanently and `llmcpp/ensure-lmstudio.sh` records why its current shape exists — a measured 14.0GB wired spike, "kernel-panic territory at 64k depth." A single `engram query` has a 1.09GB max RSS. A server whose whole value is holding the 731MB chunk store and model warm is a fourth standing claimant.

**Recommendation:** wake-on-demand, using the shape the platform already has — `votek-ensured` exists precisely because an expensive host service cannot stay resident, and `golden/pi/pi:13-18` is the client half (probe, wake, exec, never fail merely because the service was cold). The same wrapper you need for decision 9 does both jobs. **Trading away:** ~10s cold start on the first call after idle, which is the current CLI cost anyway. The thing a resident server would evict is llama-server, and every environment's harness, `check-model`, and `create_app`'s creation-time verification hang off that one service — a coupling that is invisible because the two live in different repos.

## 8. Concurrency and supervision

Both existing daemons are single-threaded stdlib `HTTPServer` (`bin/apphostd:280`, `bin/votek-ensured:71`), and task 4.0a records that as deliberate — but the rationale was about a subprocess loading a 9GB model, and it does not transfer to a read query. Three concurrent `engram query` runs completed in 12.06/12.05/12.04s against 11.93s for one alone, so the store parallelizes reads fine; serialization is a property the server would *add*. On supervision, `apphostd`'s startup guards `SystemExit` when the recorded tailnet address is not on an interface, which under `KeepAlive` becomes an undesigned 10s crash loop until tailscaled comes up — and `grep -c 'not on any interface'` on its log returns 0, so that retry behaviour is inherited, never tested.

**Recommendation:** bounded concurrency (2–3) with waits logged so a slow recall is attributable; `KeepAlive` with explicit backoff and a logged "waiting for tailnet" line rather than fail-fast; a readiness distinction so "index still loading" answers 503-with-a-reason instead of looking like an empty vault. Two operational details no existing plist handles: set `ThrottleInterval` explicitly rather than relying on launchd's 10s default, and decide log rotation — nothing rotates `~/Library/Logs`, cloudflared's is already 297KB, and one line per query per env grows without bound. Also decide explicitly whether **your** host CLI goes through the server: `README.md:286-289` makes the in-process host CLI the documented break-glass path precisely because it survives a dead daemon.

## 9. How the endpoint reaches the agent — one wrapper, and what value it carries

Four separate questions collapse into one artifact. The systemd drop-in from `write_control_config()` is wrong twice over (it configures `app.service`, and it returns early unless the app holds the single grant). Shell rc files are worse than they look: `build-golden:94-122` appends hooks in-place to `.profile`/`.bashrc`/fish config, none of which are in `golden/FILES`, and they are already fleet-inconsistent — golden installs fish and an `exec fish` hook, while `hello`, `todo` and `dash` all have `fish` MISSING and zero `exec fish` lines. `/etc/profile.d` is dead too: `build-golden:85-87` records that Tailscale SSH gives interactive *non-login* shells.

The pi wrapper is the precedent that works, and I verified its PATH precedence for both shells and services: `systemctl show-environment` inside `hello` gives `PATH=/usr/local/sbin:/usr/local/bin:...`, so `/usr/local/sbin/engram` shadows the real client for interactive shells, `ssh host cmd`, and systemd units alike.

**Recommendation:** a managed wrapper at `/usr/local/sbin/engram` in `golden/FILES`, carrying `${ENGRAM_SERVER:-…}` in `pi`'s shape, plus one small per-env override file beside it. The wrapper is hashed, drift-checked, and — the deciding advantage — deliverable by `fleet/offer` to the three envs that already exist; only the one-line override needs deliberate placement. It also carries the wake-probe (decision 7) and the degradation behaviour: recall's only failure instruction (`SKILL.md:70`) covers `engram ingest --auto` and nothing else, so behaviour on a failed `engram query` is undefined and will be improvised, and `write-memory/SKILL.md:88-91` prescribes retry-then-paste-the-error-verbatim. The wrapper should print `vault unreachable — continuing without memory` to stderr and exit 0 on *reachability* failure only, never masking a real query error, with `--version`/`--help` passthrough so `app-environments` spec.md:25-27 stays true.

On the **value**: do not bake the MagicDNS name. `tailscale status` lists both `toejough-laptop-1` (100.70.216.20) and `toejough-laptop` (100.126.28.86) — the name has already churned once, and `control_url()` (`bin/appctl_lib.py:328-348`) resolves from the recorded *address* specifically so a rename cannot silently point envs elsewhere. Put the endpoint in exactly one file; do not repeat the model endpoint's mistake of writing the same literal into both `pi` and `votek.ts`. And add a server-side guard: reject a caller whose tailnet peer is not a node this host created. A MagicDNS name is tailnet-scoped, so an env restored onto a second Mac in the same tailnet keeps working *against the original host's vault* — a silently-correct-looking wrong vault is worse than a dead endpoint, and an env-side default cannot detect that it moved.

## 10. Client binary: committed in `golden/FILES`, or self-installed — and what to ask engram for

The precedent is explicit: `golden/server/bin/serve` is a 5.4MB statically-linked aarch64 ELF committed to git, chosen in `apps-serve-a-site-not-a-repo` Decision 8 over both alternatives because building at delivery time "leaves `check-baseline` with nothing to hash in a fresh clone." Transport is a non-issue — a 32MB blob through `orb ... cat >` measured 0.120s. Self-install is currently *broken*, not merely undesirable: `go install github.com/toejough/engram/...` gets `model.onnx` as a 133-byte LFS pointer stub from the module proxy (engram's own updater documents this at `internal/update/update.go:1240-1246` and clones instead), there are no published releases, and no env has Go.

The build is the harder half. `serve` reports `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 -trimpath`; the current engram binary reports `CGO_ENABLED=1`, and the host has no Linux cross toolchain (zig, aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc, musl-gcc all missing). Two *separate* tag surfaces are needed, and conflating them is easy: `cmd/engram/hugot.go` is the only hugot importer in `main` (drop it → cgo-free), but the 87MB model lives at `internal/embed/hugot.go:271` `//go:embed assets/model/*`, which imports no hugot and survives a cgo-free build untouched.

**Recommendation:** committed in `golden/FILES`, matching `serve` — but **sequenced**: the `offer` stamp fix first (prerequisites below), then the measured size (OQ1), then the commit. Put `CGO_ENABLED=0` **plus a model-free embed** in the ask to engram, naming both file paths so the ask is actionable rather than aspirational. In the same change, write the build recipe down in this repo — `bin/build-client` covering both `serve` and the client, or at minimum the flags in `golden/*/README.md`. Today `CGO_ENABLED` appears exactly once in the whole repo, in an archived tasks note, which means the flags for the binary running in three environments survive only there. Docker is already installed, so a linux/arm64 build is one containerized `go build`, not a pipeline. **Trading away:** ~40% of the client's size in permanent git history per revision, against a repo that currently packs to 2.57 MiB, with the revision trigger owned by another repo.

## 11. Verification: what proves this works, and what the isolation check becomes

`fleet/check-isolation`'s `reach()` (`:92-100`) only ever probes `http://host.orb.internal:$port/` — one of at least five planes an env has to the host. A `CLOSED_PORTS` entry for a tailnet-bound engram would report `ok host:PORT refused` while the tailnet listener served every env. And the check currently reports **all 21 green** while `hello` reaches `todo` three ways, dash's control proxy, and eleven undeclared host ports.

That enumeration is the sharper finding, and it is already a written requirement: the isolate delta at `specs/app-environments/spec.md:22-24` promises host services are "listed from the host's own listeners rather than from memory." Nothing implements it — a repo-wide grep for `lsof|netstat|LISTEN` returns one hit, prose in a tasks file. `lsof` shows 29 listening ports, 3 decided. Probed from `hello`, twelve answered: optillm:8000, llama-server:8080 and :55251, LM Studio:41343, cloudflared:20241, lmlink:53965, EEventManager:2968, **ARDAgent:3283 (Apple Remote Desktop)**, ControlCenter:5000 and :7000 (AirPlay), rapportd:58889 (Continuity), and **OrbStack's own SSH gateway at :32222**, which returned the banner `SSH-2.0-OrbStack` to the app that is public on the internet.

**Recommendation:** three checks, all folded into the engram change except the last, which should be filed separately.
- Replace the two hardcoded port lists with the declarative table from decision 3 — `(service, port, bind plane, expected answer for a granted env, expected answer for a non-granted env)` — and make `reach()` take the plane as an argument. For a non-granted env, assert 403 *on the plane engram binds* **and** connection-refused on `host.orb.internal`, so a future loopback fallback cannot reopen it silently. Assert on a read endpoint, not just `/`: with #720 removing the bearer token, the 8092-era "403 even holding a valid credential" has no analogue — its replacement is "refused before any vault content is read."
- `fleet/check-engram` in the `check-model` mould, plus a creation-time check alongside `check_harness()` at `bin/appctl_lib.py:581`. ## 12. Prerequisites and sequencing — what must land before the first `golden/FILES` entry

Three of these are not engram's work and all three break the delivery story engram depends on.

**`fleet/offer` never stamps.** It writes, chmods, re-hashes, prints success, and never touches `/etc/apphost-baseline.json`. So a newly-managed file goes `missing` → delivered → `current` → and at the next baseline bump `differs` (because `classify()` sees `built_hash is None`, `_baseline.py:107`), which `offer` refuses (`:83-88`). `fleet/adopt` cannot rescue it — it early-returns on any machine that already has a stamp. This is live: `hello`'s stamp has 5 entries and **none** of the five `/app/server/*` paths, all of which `check-baseline` reports as `current`. Five platform files in `hello` are already un-deliverable on their next revision. Adding a fast-moving multi-megabyte artifact to a mechanism that can deliver each file once per pre-existing env is the wrong order of operations. **Fix `offer` to record what it delivered** — a few lines, honest, and it retroactively unblocks `hello`'s five.

**`fleet/check-baseline --start-stopped` crashes.** Verified: `ORB` is used at lines 62 and 79 and is not in the import at `:32-33`. Without the flag, the stopped-template path prints `skip stopped` and exits **0** having verified nothing. So the golden template — the one machine whose staleness every future app inherits — has never been checked, and README's documented post-`golden/` workflow passes green on a template it never opened. Survivable today only because `build-golden:64-74` stamps at build time. One-line fix; make the no-flag skip loud.

**Order the changes.** Land `host-lmstudio-extension` first: it is unblocked, narrow, renames the `votek` surface engram would otherwise be written against, and establishes the exact "a platform file supplies the default and the owner's own configuration outranks it" pattern engram's wrapper should reuse. Do **not** gate engram on `bin-serve-is-the-entry-point` (blocked on the dash repo, no shared surface). The real overlaps are `README.md:168` inside the trust-boundary paragraph (its task 2.6), `bin/appctl_lib.py:443` (its task 2.3), and `golden/FILES` — not `check-isolation`, which that change never touches.

**Three text fixes, cheap now and expensive later.** (a) Edit the isolate delta scenario at `specs/app-environments/spec.md:18-20` **before archiving** — the requirement at `:4` already says "offers *it*" (per-environment), so only the scenario enumerates today's two instances and will be false the day a selectively-offered service lands. One scenario edit; no new capability, no `host-services` capability yet. (b) Discharge task 6.1 in place with an inline note, ruling `mounts` out on **testability** grounds: `mounts` appears nowhere in `bin/` or `fleet/`, `_assert_isolated()` probes three fixed paths and `check-isolation:58` four, so a vault mounted anywhere else passes every check the platform has — plus it grants files rather than query capability (844MB, of which 731MB is chunk index, and unusable without the embedding model). That also resolves the standing contradiction between `proposal.md:105-109`, which blesses `mounts`, and the delta scenario, which says no such path exists. (c) `README.md:140-142` and `:166-171` still describe the pre-4.2 world ("`:8092` and `:8091` both still answer every environment... a bearer token defends `:8092`"), and the reach table at `:155-163` omits `:8091` entirely — the section is wrong in both directions. Give the table a "granted to" column so engram is a row that says *per-environment grant* rather than silently reading as fleet-wide.

**One more thing not to do:** do not add a fifth hand-placed LaunchAgent. `git ls-files | grep -i plist` is empty; the four host plists exist only in `~/Library/LaunchAgents`, unversioned and uncheckable, and README:304-307 already documents only three of them. `dev.toejough.apphostd.plist` runs the daemon straight out of the working tree. # Open questions — blocked on a fact, with the measurement that resolves each

**OQ1 — What does a client-only engram binary weigh?** Gates decision 10 entirely and the git-cost objection with it. Anchors: the current darwin binary is 118,604,354 bytes; embedded assets are 90,886,144; so non-asset code is ~27.7MB. onnxruntime contributes essentially nothing (it is `dlopen`'d at runtime, `yalue/onnxruntime_go setup_env.go:68`), so what a CGO-free client sheds is the tokenizers cgo archive plus hugot's Go code — plausibly landing anywhere from ~10MB to ~27MB. **Measurement:** one `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=linux GOARCH=arm64 -trimpath -ldflags='-s -w'` build with the model embed tagged out; report stripped and gzipped size. Under ~10MB the committed answer is obvious; near ~27MB with frequent rebuilds, a *published release artifact* earns a hearing. Do not settle the vehicle before this lands. (Corollary the same build resolves: onnxruntime being `dlopen`'d means a cgo engram inside a VM would additionally need a `libonnxruntime.so` no env has — an independent reason the client build is necessary, not merely smaller.)

**OQ2 — Does `orb config set machine.<name>.isolate_network true` close bridge reach without breaking Tailscale, ingress, or `host.orb.internal`?** Gates decision 2 and therefore the grant model. **Measurement:** flip it on a throwaway machine the way task 0.1 did, then re-run the four cross-app probes. Note it almost certainly does *not* close the host's `*:8080` wildcard forward, which is governed by `machines.expose_ports_to_lan` and is outside any ACL — so plan on needing two answers, not one.

**OQ3 — Are tailnet nodes ephemeral, and can a freed name be claimed?** This decides how strong the peer-address → app-name mapping actually is, which everything about provenance rests on. `isotest`, created and `orb delete`d during task 2.2, is gone from `tailscale status` and no longer resolves — good, but it also suggests the OAuth-derived join may produce *ephemeral* nodes, in which case a merely **stopped** app loses its node too and `rmapp` (which stops and never deletes) frees a name within minutes. That inverts which operation is dangerous. **Three measurements:** (a) check the OAuth client's configuration in the Tailscale admin console, or create a throwaway, stop it, and watch `tailscale status`; (b) from a throwaway env, attempt `tailscale up --hostname=<a freed app name>` with the key as it exists inside that env and see whether it lands or gets suffixed; (c) determine whether the `tskey-client-…` OAuth secret is *recoverable from inside a running env* after creation — grep the env's filesystem, shell history and journal for `tskey-`. "It passed through the env at creation" and "an agent can read it today" are different threats and only the second makes a name-claim attack self-service. One thing is already resolved and needs no work: a name with **no** node fails closed (`getaddrinfo` raises → empty frozenset → 403), so reconciling the allowlist against `apps()` would be effort spent on the safe case. Reconcile for *re-claimed* names instead.

**OQ4 — Does Tailscale SSH support remote port forwarding?** The only unknown that decides whether decision 1's cheap shape exists at all: access present in the env only for the life of an owner-authenticated connection, no listener, no grant file. `orb config show` reveals a per-machine `forward_ssh_agent` knob (false everywhere), so session-scoped plumbing is a dimension the platform already has and does not use. **Measurement:** a ten-minute test from the host. It was not run.

**OQ5 — How many `show-chunk` calls does one real deep recall actually issue?** Half of this is already answered and it matters: the ~10s per-call cost is **per-process init, not per-lookup** — `engram show-chunk /nonexistent/path#turn-999999` prints "chunk not found" and still costs 10.13s real / 7.71s user, identical to a successful lookup, while `engram show` on a note is 0.07s. So a long-lived (or woken) server pays it once and each env-side `show-chunk` becomes a ~30ms round trip; the "a 731MB scan per call means no server fixes it" branch is closed. What remains: recall's `SKILL.md:161` says "process every cluster" with no cap, and a 3-phrase query already returns 88 chunk items. **Measurement:** instrument one real deep recall on the host and count actual `show-chunk` invocations. If it's five, this is a footnote. Do not ship a glance-only restriction to environments on the strength of the CLI's numbers — the CLI is paying a startup tax the server will not.

**OQ6 — Does engram want to serve the agent instructions, or wire `DeployModeManifest`?** This is an ask, not a measurement, but it blocks decision on how skills reach an env. `engram update` is host-only under #720 and impractical in an env regardless: all three harness specs use `DeployModeSymlink` from a source tree, and remote mode does `git clone` + LFS smudge + `go install`, needing Go and git-lfs — both MISSING in `hello`. But engram *does* have a copy-based `DeployModeManifest` (`update.go:34-47`, `:622-632`) that no supported harness selects, so wiring it is a smaller ask than it looks. Meanwhile no env has `/root/.claude/skills` or `/root/.pi/agent/skills` at all, and `/root/.claude` is currently your territory — `hello` and `todo` each hold a hand-written `settings.json`, `dash` has no `/root/.claude`. **Recommendation while you wait:** ship the minimal 8 files (recall/learn/write-memory `SKILL.md` = 42,349 bytes, three guidance snippets, two commands — *not* the `tests/` trees) as platform files, with an explicit `golden/FILES` comment saying they mirror another repo, the same honesty the `serve` entry shows. Never bring `/root/.claude/settings.json` under management: it would classify `differs` in both envs (no stamp entry exists) and `offer` would refuse it forever. Decide this before the binary ships — "we'll add the skills later" is how a client nobody calls becomes permanent.

# Already settled — looks like a decision, isn't

**S1. Bind the tailnet with a peer check. There is no viable loopback variant.** `host.orb.internal` re-originates, so a loopback-bound service sees every caller as 127.0.0.1 — that is *no* policy, not weak policy, and it forecloses provenance entirely, which #720 explicitly rejects. The bridge preserves peer identity but nothing inside a machine resolves to `192.168.139.3`, so it is a raw DHCP IP per env — the staleness apphostd's grant-by-name design exists to avoid. And the loopback port set has drifted from 3 decided to 29 listening in four weeks. Settled empirically, not by argument: from `hello`, `100.70.216.20:8092` returns 403 with `remote_ip=100.70.216.20`, while `host.orb.internal:8092` is refused outright.

**S2. No new bearer credential.** Issue #2's direction — the peer check is the whole boundary — is settled, and engram should depend on the sentence #2 writes rather than inventing a second phrasing. Do not bundle #2's amendment to `platform-control-api:6-7` into the engram change.

**S3. Record the bind address and verify it; never re-derive it.** `bin/apphostd:229-268` documents three tried-and-wrong answers: `os.uname()` binds a *different* device (tailscale suffixes on collision — this host is `toejough-laptop-1`); guessing from interfaces is ambiguous (100.70.216.20 on en0, 100.126.28.86 on en3); and the Tailscale.app CLI under launchd prints `CLIError error 3` to stdout with exit 0, so the daemon binds the error string — its log holds eight cycles of exactly that. The settled rule: record in config, verify against `ifconfig` at startup, refuse to start on mismatch, never fall back to loopback. **Two open sub-parts inside the settled rule, neither of which is engram's to solve:** the file is `~/.config/apphost/control-addr`, read in exactly three places, and its name says "control" — three readers is the cheapest a rename will ever be. And the verification regex (`:263`) and the bind (`:280`) are IPv4-only while the host holds a tailnet IPv6; harmless today only because the env's resolver returns an A record, and this platform has had that resolver break once. **Enforcement note:** you cannot share this code with engram — it is Go in another repo, apphostd is Python here. Own it on this side: have the LaunchAgent invoke a host wrapper that reads the file, verifies, exits non-zero on mismatch, and only then execs `engram serve --bind <addr>`.

**S4. Transport is free; the cost is host CPU, and it is per-process.** A 3-phrase `engram query --lazy-chunks` costs 11.93s real / 9.47s user and returns 127KB; a tailnet round trip from `hello` measures 3.5–18ms. Payload trimming, compression and binary protocols are optimizing well under 1% of the total. The design budget goes to residency (decision 7) and serialization (decision 8), and nothing else.

**S5. The vault contains no credential-shaped material today** — 16 patterns, all zero across ~700 notes. Settled *as of now*; keep it settled with the standing check in decision 6, because the whole-vault answer rests on it.

**S6. `mounts` is out.** Not because the delta scenario forbids it — that text contradicts the same change's own proposal — but because it cannot be asserted: `mounts` appears in no executable code in this repo, neither isolation probe reads `orb config`, and a mount at any path outside those seven hardcoded strings passes everything. Add the mechanical reasons (844MB with no verb granularity, unusable without the embedding model, host filesystem back inside an env) and this is a decision with a stated basis rather than a text conflict.

**S7. A tailnet ACL cannot express per-app engram policy, and could not fix cross-app reach anyway.** `join_tailnet()` advertises one `tag:apps` for the whole fleet (`bin/appctl_lib.py:324`), and ACLs are source-based, so the only tailnet-layer control is all-apps-or-none. Per-app tags are the structurally right answer eventually, but they make app creation depend on a tailnet policy write (advertising a tag that doesn't exist makes `tailscale up` fail), and they would close only the MagicDNS path — the bridge and the host's wildcard forward are outside Tailscale entirely. So the application-layer peer check is the whole boundary, alone, exactly as `bin/apphostd:17-19` warns. Two things to write down rather than leave implicit: a coarse `tag:apps → host:<engram-port>` rule is fine, and your own devices ("the owner's personal devices may read and write, attributed as the owner") need an identity mapping or `/learn` from your phone lands unattributed.

**S8. You cannot condition the grant on how capable the agent is.** Both items that discounted the exfiltration risk reasoned from `qwen/qwen3.5-9b` — true for pi, and they checked only pi. `hello` — the app that is public on the internet — holds `/root/.claude/.credentials.json` (509 bytes, 0600, Aug 3) and `settings.json` naming `"model": "sonnet"`; `todo` holds the same with `"advisorModel": "opus"`. Neither has a `permissions` block, both have full outbound internet. A credential can appear via `/login` at any moment with no platform involvement and nothing checks for it. That pushes the answer toward per-verb scoping (decision 4) and the consumer question (decision 1), and away from any policy that reasons about what the reader can do.

**S9. Concurrent reads parallelize at the store.** Three simultaneous queries: 12.06/12.05/12.04s, total wall 12.07s. Serialization would be something the server *adds*, so single-threading is a choice to justify, not a default to inherit.

**S10. The isolate delta's requirement already permits selective offering.** `specs/app-environments/spec.md:4` says a service the platform "deliberately offers **it**" — per-environment. No new `host-services` capability is needed now; only the scenario at `:18-20` lags. Revisit the capability question when the decision table from decision 3 exists, since at that point there is a real artifact to write requirements about.

`check_harness(name)` takes any machine name and works against any existing env today — `check_harness('hello')` runs right now. So delta `spec.md:4`'s "The same verification SHALL be runnable against any existing environment at any time" adds no obligation that wasn't already true when the incident occurred. (Not fully vacuous: the "halves of one harness disagree" scenario, spec.md:22-24, is genuinely new content the current check does not satisfy.)

### 3. The empirical record: this exact remedy was already tried and failed in 24 hours
Commit `9d783a9` — the "drift can't hide again" commit the proposal quotes — already did group 5's work at creation time: *"newapp now verifies the env's harness can reach the service and that the configured default is actually offered; both failure directions tested (stale name, service down)."* A correct check, tested in both failure directions, with no trigger. The identical failure recurred the next day. This is not a theoretical objection; it is a measured recurrence inside this repo.

### 4. Live proof that an uninvoked check does not merely fail to fire — it rots
`bin/appctl_lib.py:21` still reads `MODEL_SERVICE = "http://host.orb.internal:8090"`, and `:511` `MODEL_HEALTH = "http://127.0.0.1:8090/health"`. Group 1 did not touch this file (`b15073d` = `golden/pi/*` only; `aac9aa7` = `bin/votek-ensured`, tasks.md, workspace.json).

Verified read-only, from inside the env, the same way `check_harness` does it:
```
orb -m hello -u root: http://host.orb.internal:8090/v1/models → connection refused
                      http://host.orb.internal:1234/v1/models → 8 models
```
Host `lsof`: LM Studio on `127.0.0.1:1234`, Python on `8091`/`8092`; **nothing on 8090**. Post-group-1 baseline (`golden/pi/pi:10`, `golden/pi/votek.ts:14`) points both halves at `:1234`.

So the platform's model-reachability verifier — the one the base spec says makes reachability "verified when the environment is created rather than assumed," and the one 5.1 promises to make fleet-wide — is itself pointed at the dead endpoint and would report all three **working** environments as unreachable. It went stale unnoticed for precisely the reason the finding names.

### 5. A consequence the original finding missed: group 5 has no green-direction test
tasks.md:77-79 (5.3) tests only the RED direction ("point one half at a dead port… confirm the check reports it"). A check that reports *every* environment as unreachable — which `check_harness` does today — **passes 5.3**. Group 3 has the corresponding guard (3.2: "agrees with 1.2's hand-recorded answer"); group 5 has no equivalent, so the stale `:8090` target would propagate fleet-wide and validate.

### What I refute in the finding
- **The Decision-1 hypocrisy argument is weaker than claimed.** design.md:44-46 rejects a version counter because a forgotten bump makes the record *lie* (false "current"); a forgotten *run* makes the detector *silent*. Silence is a lesser failure than a false green, so that is not a strict self-contradiction — it is a different failure class. The rhetorical flourish should be dropped; the structural claim does not depend on it.
- **Surfacing was not overlooked.** design.md:132-133 raises "whether `dash` should show drift" as an Open Question and defers it to dash's repo. But an Open Question is "undecided," not "knowingly left open," and proposal.md's Deliberately-not-in-scope (lines 62-67) covers only automatic *updates* — applying, not detecting. The finding's third remedy is therefore still unmet.

### The "bind it to something that already runs" option is concrete here
`bin/apphostd:96-97` already serves `GET /apps?reachable=1` → `lib.inventory(include_reachability=True)`, which iterates every env with a per-env probe and is the endpoint dash polls; `GET /model` already returns `model_healthy()`. PROOF THAT CLONE TRANSMITS SYSTEM FILES: hello's /etc/systemd/system/app.service hashes ddfb134c… identical to repo golden/app.service, with mtime 2026-08-01 12:39:14 — installed into golden BEFORE hello was cloned at 12:43-12:45, and create_app never installs app.service; all of hello/todo/dash share root-fs birth 2026-08-01 12:29:04 with the golden snapshot. Inferring from existing clones is the wrong target: today's three apps were all cloned from one 2026-08-01 12:29 snapshot and none post-dates a golden change, so their contents say nothing about what a clone made today receives.

dispatch_events.description: Check if skills/hooks can trigger compaction
dispatch_events.prompt_text: In Claude Code (the CLI tool), is there a way for a skill or a hook to programmatically trigger context compaction (like the /compact command does)? Check for any hook events, tool, or documented mechanism that lets a hook or skill invoke compaction, or force it to happen. Report concisely — under 150 words — with a direct yes/no and specifics (event names, tool names, config) if it exists.

completion_report:
**No.** Hooks and skills cannot programmatically trigger context compaction.

**Available compaction mechanisms:**
- **`/compact` command** – manual, user-initiated only
- **PreCompact/PostCompact hooks** – *react* to compaction (fire before/after), they do not initiate it
- **`SessionStart` matcher `"compact"`** – detects when a session started via compaction, not a trigger mechanism

Compaction is user-driven via the CLI command. Hooks cannot invoke `/compact` or force the harness to compact—they only hook into the lifecycle before and after user-triggered compaction occurs.

If you need automatic compaction, that's a feature request; there's no documented or undocumented programmatic API for it.

## Middle-tier open-weight LLM for a 16GB M1 Pro — July 2026 findings

### Winner: Qwen3.5-4B (Reasoning)
- **AA Intelligence Index: 20** (independent, Artificial Analysis) — ranked #20/130; nearly matches Qwen3.5-9B Reasoning (AA 21) at half the size, and far above the "comparable model average of 9". [AA model page](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-5-4b)
- **Params:** 4.7B total, dense (all active). Multimodal input (text/image/video), 262k context, released March 2026.
- **4-bit file: ~2.5 GB** (independent, [InsiderLLM Mac guide](https://insiderllm.com/guides/best-local-llms-mac-2026/)) — well under the 4GB cap, leaves headroom for long context on 16GB.
- **MLX quants (exact repos):** [lmstudio-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/lmstudio-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit) and [mlx-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit).
- **Mac speed:** independent guides list Qwen3.5-4B at 25-35 tok/s generic Apple Silicon (InsiderLLM); [Will It Run AI](https://willitrunai.com/blog/qwen-3-5-mlx-apple-silicon-guide) reports base M1 running the **9B** at ~30 tok/s via MLX, implying the 4B lands roughly 40-55 tok/s on M1 Pro — squarely in the 35-60 target. No published M1-Pro-specific number found; [llmcheck.net](https://llmcheck.net/benchmarks) has no M1 MLX entry for it. GPQA/MMLU-Pro sub-scores are inside AA's index but not published as discrete numbers on the page.
- **Caveat:** reasoning mode spends thinking tokens, so wall-clock latency per answer is higher than tok/s suggests; non-reasoning mode is available in the same weights.

### Runner-up: Gemma 4 E4B
- **AA Intelligence Index: 12 (Reasoning)** (independent, [AA](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/gemma-4-e4b)) — clearly above LFM2.5-8B-A1B (~8) but well below Qwen3.5-4B.
- **Params:** 4B *effective* (Per-Layer Embeddings architecture); 128k context; native audio+image+video input — the only model in this band with audio. Released March 31, 2026 (vendor, [Gemma 4 guide](https://aurigait.com/blog/gemma-4-features-benchmarks-guide/)).
- **4-bit file: ~5 GB** — slightly over the 4GB cap but fine in 16GB RAM.
- **MLX repos:** [mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-4bit](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-4bit), [mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-OptiQ-4bit](https://huggingface.co/mlx-community/gemma-4-e4b-it-OptiQ-4bit), [unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-UD-MLX-4bit](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-E4B-it-UD-MLX-4bit).
- **Mac speed:** 25-40 tok/s generic (independent, InsiderLLM). Note: there is **no plain "Gemma 4 4B"** — the family is E2B / E4B / 12B / 26B-A4B / 31B; the 26B-A4B MoE (AA 26, 3.8B active) is the smart one but its ~13GB Q4 file blows the budget ([AA small models](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/open-source/small)).

### Wildcard: G9v3-3B (AI9Stars)
**AA 16**, 3B dense, 130k ctx, reasoning model ([AA](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/g9v3-3b), [HF](https://huggingface.co/ai9stars/G9v3-3B)) — second-smartest in-band and would be fast (~3B dense), but **no MLX quant found** on lmstudio-community/mlx-community as of this search. Watch for quants; would displace Gemma 4 E4B if they land.

### Evaluated and eliminated
| Model | Why out |
|---|---|
| **Llama 4 "8B"** | Does not exist — Llama 4 is only Scout 109B-A17B / Maverick 400B-A17B ([Thunder Compute](https://www.thundercompute.com/blog/llama-4-ai-model-ollama)) |
| **Ling/Ring-mini-2.0** (16B-A1.4B) | Sept/Oct 2025 vintage, no 2026 mini refresh (2.5/2.6 lines are 1T-scale only); Q4 file ~8-9GB breaks the 4GB cap ([HF](https://huggingface.co/inclusionAI/Ring-mini-2.0), [Ant release](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/ant-group-releases-ling-2-100100729.html)) |
| **IBM Granite 4.1 3B** | AA 5 — below the LFM2.5 floor ([AA tiny models](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/open-source/tiny)) |
| **Granite 4 Small** (32B-A9B) | File size far over budget for 16GB |
| **Phi-4 Mini 3.8B** | AA 6 — too weak; **Phi-5 not yet released** (pre-announcement only, [Spheron](https://www.spheron.network/blog/deploy-phi-5-gpu-cloud/)); no Phi-4.5 exists |
| **Liquid LFM2-24B-A2B** | Newest bigger Liquid (24B total, 2B active) — ~12-13GB Q4, targets 32GB RAM (vendor, [Liquid blog](https://www.liquid.ai/blog/lfm2-24b-a2b)) |
| **Qwen3.6-35B-A3B** (AA 32, 3B active) | Smartest MoE in the active-param band but 36B total ≈ 19.5GB Q4 — doesn't fit 16GB |
| **NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano 4B** | AA 9 — barely above the floor, dominated by Qwen3.5-4B |

### Bottom line
**Qwen3.5-4B (thinking) via lmstudio-community/Qwen3.5-4B-MLX-4bit** is the clear winner: AA 20 (vs Liquid's ~8 floor and the 9B's 21), ~2.5GB file, dense 4.7B so expect roughly 1.7-2x the 9B's 24-29 tok/s on M1 Pro MLX. Runner-up **Gemma 4 E4B** (AA 12) only if you want audio/multimodal input or Gemma's ecosystem. No published M1-Pro-specific tok/s benchmark exists for either — verify locally with `mlx_lm.generate` before committing.
